references.text: Jesus quotes this very passage from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth (Isa 61:1–2) and declares that the Scripture is now fulfilled in the ears of his listeners.
The immediate context where Jesus reads from the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue, which he then declares fulfilled in verse 21.
Jesus says he has not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them—the same principle of scriptural fulfillment as in Luke 4:21.
Jesus describes his ministry with reference to Isaiah’s prophecies—the blind see, the lame walk, and the lepers are cleansed—as signs that the prophecies are fulfilled.
The risen Jesus explains that everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled—the same theme of scriptural fulfillment.
Paul proclaims that the promise God gave to the fathers he has now fulfilled for us their children by raising up Jesus—fulfillment of Scripture as a central theme.
Jesus sends word to John that the blind see, the lame walk, and the poor have the gospel preached to them—a direct fulfillment of the Isaiah prophecy he read in Nazareth.
Peter speaks of the prophetic word made firm, on which it is wise to keep one’s attention—the fulfillment of Scripture as a central theme connected with Jesus’ coming.
Isaiah speaks of the Lord’s servant who will bring justice to the nations, open blind eyes, and lead captives out of prison—prophecies that Jesus declares fulfilled in himself.
